hub.description: Decks and fences in Smyrna, TN, planned for newer HOA subdivisions, sloped lots near Percy Priest Lake, and families who work shifts.
hub.intro: Many Smyrna homes were built in the last twenty years. If yours is one of them, the backyard probably sits inside a subdivision with an HOA, and the lawn is whatever the builder graded and sodded. Part of Percy Priest Lake reaches inside town limits, and some lots near it slope toward the water. A lot of households here also work shifts at the Nissan plant or somewhere else, and that matters when a crew shows up to dig post holes. This page gives a short overview of decks and fences in Smyrna, with a full page on each service.

sections.heading: What a newer Smyrna backyard usually looks like
paragraphs: Across Smyrna, plenty of houses from the last two decades came with a small builder deck or only a concrete pad and a few steps at the back door. The yard behind it was shaped to move water toward a swale along the side or rear line. Keep that swale in mind early. A fence that dams it or a deck that sits in its path can leave you with standing water after a heavy rain, and water pushed onto the next lot can turn into a dispute with a neighbor.

Under the sod, many Smyrna yards have stiff clay, and limestone often sits close to the surface in this part of Rutherford County. Neither one stops a project. Both change how footings and post holes get dug. Before you accept a firm price from anyone, ask how the bid handles rock if the auger hits it close to the surface.

sections.heading: Decks for Smyrna homes
paragraphs: Deck work in Smyrna usually falls into two camps. One is the first real deck on a house that only had a stoop or a small platform. The other is replacing a builder deck that has reached the age where boards go soft and railings start to move. In both cases the height of the back door and the grade under it shape the design before anyone picks a board. Our [Smyrna deck builder page](/deck-builder-smyrna-tn/) goes deeper on footings and permits, and on decks for lots that drop toward the lake.

sections.heading: Fences for Smyrna yards
paragraphs: Wood privacy fences are common in Smyrna subdivisions. Most people want one to keep a dog in or to put some distance between the patio and the house behind them. In an HOA community, the covenants often control the style and height, and some limit how far toward the street a fence can run. Lots that back up to common ground or a drainage area raise their own questions about where your property really ends. The [Smyrna fence company page](/fence-company-smyrna-tn/) covers post setting and property lines in detail.

sections.heading: Sloped yards on the lake side of Smyrna
paragraphs: In parts of Smyrna, some homes sit close enough to Percy Priest Lake that the backyard runs downhill toward the water. A deck on that kind of lot can be close to the ground at the door and well up in the air at the far end, which calls for taller posts with more bracing and usually a stair down to the yard. A fence on the same slope has to step down or follow the grade. Much of the land along the shoreline is managed by the Army Corps of Engineers, so your deed line may stop short of the water. Clearing or building on Corps land takes their permission, if it is allowed at all.

sections.heading: Planning around shift work
paragraphs: Smyrna is home to the Nissan assembly plant, and many families here have someone on nights or rotating shifts. That affects a build more than people expect. Digging post holes and cutting lumber are loud, and the noise carries into a bedroom where someone is trying to sleep at noon. If that is your house, mention it when you ask for an estimate so timing is part of the conversation from the start. Shifts also shape the design. A deck that mostly gets used in the morning after a night shift may need shade from a different side than one used on weekend evenings.

sections.heading: HOA review and town permits
paragraphs: Whether you live in Ashton Park or on a street near Smyrna Town Centre, find out early whether covenants apply to your lot. Many Smyrna subdivisions have an architectural review step, and the committee usually wants a drawing and a site plan before it signs off. That approval is separate from any permit. Attached or raised decks usually need a permit, and fences sometimes do. Homes inside town limits work with the Town of Smyrna, while homes outside town limits go through Rutherford County. Rules vary, so check with the right codes office and your HOA. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) shows how to put together a clean submission.

faqs.q: Do I need HOA approval before a deck or fence goes in?
faqs.a: If your home is in one of the many Smyrna subdivisions with covenants, probably yes. Most HOAs want to review fences and decks before work starts, even ones that sit entirely in the backyard. Look in your covenants or on the HOA website for an architectural review form. Give the review some time, and do not let anyone start digging until you have the approval in writing.

faqs.q: Our yard runs down toward Percy Priest Lake. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Not usually. Many lots on the lake side of Smyrna slope, and both decks and fences can be built on them. The slope changes the work. Deck posts get taller and need more bracing, and fence sections step down the hill instead of running straight. The bigger question is often where your property ends. If Corps of Engineers land sits between you and the water, find that line before planning anything near it.

faqs.q: I work nights. Can the project be scheduled around my sleep?
faqs.a: Mention your schedule when you ask for an estimate so it is part of the plan from the start. The loudest part of a deck or fence job is the digging and cutting early on. Some families plan those days for when the sleeper is off or staying elsewhere, and quieter tasks can often fill the rest. Plenty of Smyrna households deal with this because of shift work, so it is a normal thing to ask.

deck.description: Deck builder in Smyrna, TN for aging builder decks, first decks on newer subdivision homes, and sloped lots near Percy Priest Lake.
deck.intro: In a ten or twenty year old Smyrna house, the back door often opens onto a small builder deck that is starting to wear, or onto a couple of concrete steps and a patch of grass. Either one is a fine place to start. What we build next depends mostly on the ground under the yard and the rules in your subdivision. Below is how a deck builder should think through both in Smyrna before drawing anything.

sections.heading: Replacing an aging builder deck in Smyrna
paragraphs: The subdivisions that filled in around Smyrna over the last twenty years brought a lot of small builder decks with them. Many were framed with pressure treated pine and built just big enough for a grill and a couple of chairs. Those decks are now old enough to show it. Boards cup and split, and the railing posts start to rock when you lean on them. Some only need new boards. Others have rot where it matters most.

Start at the ledger, the board where the deck attaches to the house. Then look at the bottoms of the posts and at any joist under a board that feels soft. Rot in those spots means the frame is done, even if the top looks decent. For a closer look before you call anyone, our guide on [signs your deck is done](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) walks through what to check. A replacement is also a chance to fix a builder deck that was always too small for a table and chairs.

sections.heading: What is under a Smyrna backyard
paragraphs: Much of Rutherford County sits on limestone, and in many Smyrna yards the rock is not far below the grass. Above it there is usually a layer of dense clay that swells when it is wet and shrinks when it dries out in late summer. Deck footings have to rest on stable ground below that movement. When the digger hits rock early, the footing may need to be drilled into the rock or shifted a little, and the beam layout can change to match.

Clay also holds water. In a newer subdivision, the topsoil was often scraped off during grading, and the ground right next to the foundation is usually loose backfill. That soil can be softer than it looks. Footings belong on undisturbed soil or rock, never on fill. That is why the ground gets checked before the layout is final, and why a fair bid on a Smyrna deck should say in writing what happens if rock turns up.

sections.heading: Decks on lake lots near Percy Priest
paragraphs: Smyrna homes that sit near Percy Priest Lake often have backyards that fall away from the house. A deck there may start a step down from the back door and end with the outer rim well above the grass. Posts get longer and need bracing so the deck does not sway. Guardrails and stairs become a bigger part of the design and the budget. Plan the stair landing so it drops you somewhere useful, not into the wettest part of the slope.

Lake lots bring a property line question too. The Army Corps of Engineers manages much of the land around Percy Priest, and the strip between a yard and the water is often public land. A deck has to sit fully on your side of that line, and trees on Corps land should not be cut to open up a view. Check your plat or survey before the design starts. When the view is the whole point, a deck set a little higher or turned slightly on the lot can often do more than cutting anything down.

sections.heading: HOA review and permits for a Smyrna deck
paragraphs: Most newer Smyrna subdivisions have covenants, and many send deck plans through an architectural review committee. Rules differ from one subdivision to the next, so a deck you saw near Stewart Creek says little about what your own HOA will approve. Expect to submit a drawing that shows the size of the deck and where it sits on the lot. Some committees also ask about railing style or stain color so the deck fits the rest of the street. Review can take a while, so file before you are in a hurry. A good deck builder will help you put the drawing together, though the request usually has to come from you as the owner.

The permit is a separate step. Decks attached to a house or built off the ground usually need one, and an inspector typically looks at the footings and framing along the way. Inside town limits that means the Town of Smyrna. Homes just outside Smyrna town limits deal with Rutherford County instead. Rules and fees vary, so confirm with the codes office that covers your address. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how inspections usually work.

sections.heading: A deck for the hours you are actually home
paragraphs: Plenty of Smyrna families keep hours set by a plant shift instead of a nine to five. That changes how a deck gets used. If you come home in the morning after working nights, a deck on the east side of the house gets hot and bright right when you want to sit outside and wind down. For someone who works days and grills after dark, stair lighting and a clear path to the yard matter more than the view. Think about when you are actually out there, and share that when you ask for an estimate, since it affects which way the deck should face.

sections.heading: Choosing boards for sun and shade
paragraphs: Pressure treated pine is the common starting point in Smyrna subdivisions. It costs less up front, and it needs cleaning and a coat of sealer or stain every few years to stay in good shape. Composite boards need less upkeep, though they still want an occasional cleaning, and they can get hot underfoot on a deck that takes full afternoon sun. A deck on the shady side of the house stays damp longer, which invites mildew on any surface. Our guide to [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) goes further, including how each one looks after a few Tennessee summers.

faqs.q: Can I keep the frame of my old builder deck and only replace the boards?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the ledger is bolted and flashed and the posts are solid where they meet the ground, new boards on the old frame can make sense. Some builder decks around Smyrna fail that test, usually at the ledger or at the post bases. Putting new boards on a weak frame just hides the problem for a while. Have the frame checked first so you know which way to go.

faqs.q: Does a deck in Smyrna need a permit if it is attached to the house?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Attached decks and decks raised off the ground are the ones codes offices care about most, because the ledger and the railings carry real safety risk. The office you deal with depends on whether your address is inside Smyrna town limits or out in the county. Rules change and differ between offices, so call before the work starts. An unpermitted deck can also cause trouble when you sell the house.

faqs.q: Our Smyrna lot slopes down toward the lake. What changes with a tall deck?
faqs.a: More of the budget goes into the structure you never walk on, and less into the part you do. A long stair down to the yard adds up quickly, as does the guardrail around a high platform. The inspector will look closely at all of it. On a steep lot it can be worth talking about a lower deck with a wider stair to the yard, which sometimes gives you more usable space than one big platform high in the air.

faqs.q: How big should a new deck be on a smaller subdivision lot?
faqs.a: Start with what you want to put on it. A table for six and a grill need more room than two chairs, and the path from the door to the stairs needs space of its own. On a tight Smyrna lot, setbacks and the drainage swale can limit where the deck goes. Think too about how much grass you want left for kids or a dog. Your HOA may have its own limits as well.

faqs.q: Will a composite deck get too hot in a Smyrna summer?
faqs.a: It can. Composite boards, especially darker colors, soak up afternoon sun and can be uncomfortable barefoot on a west facing deck in July. Lighter colors help, and so does shade from the house or a tree. Wood gets warm too, but usually less so. If the deck faces west and you plan to use it on summer afternoons, bring this up with any deck builder you talk to before picking a board.

fence.description: Fence installation in Smyrna, TN: privacy fences that fit HOA covenants, posts set in clay and rock, and lake lot lines checked before digging.
fence.intro: If you live in one of the Smyrna subdivisions built over the last twenty years, you know how close the backyards sit. They line up against each other, and there is often a neighbor's deck looking right down into yours. The HOA usually has rules about what a fence can look like. A privacy fence handles most of that, as long as it goes in on the right line and meets the covenants. This page covers fence installation in Smyrna from the ground up, including lake lots near Percy Priest and homes where someone sleeps during the day.

sections.heading: Privacy fences in Smyrna subdivisions
paragraphs: In many Smyrna neighborhoods, the covenants spell out what a fence can look like. Common rules cover height and material, and many also say which side of the fence faces out. Some communities want the fence to start at or behind the back corner of the house instead of running toward the front. Others prefer a matching style so the backyards read as one line from the street. Read the covenants before you pick a design. It saves a round of revisions with the review committee.

The usual choice is a wood privacy fence, either board on board or a simpler stockade style with the finished side facing out. Board on board costs more, but the overlapping pickets leave no gaps as the wood shrinks. Shadowbox, with boards alternating on each side of the rail, lets some air through while still blocking most views. Horizontal boards give a more modern look. Some HOAs only allow one or two styles, so check yours before you settle on one. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares these styles side by side.

sections.heading: Finding the property line before digging
paragraphs: Whether the house is in Hickory Hills or a few blocks from Smyrna Town Centre, the line comes first. Newer subdivisions have one advantage here, since the lots were surveyed fairly recently and the corner pins are often still in the ground, even if they are buried under sod or mulch. Your closing papers may include a plat or a survey that shows the lines. If the pins cannot be found, a surveyor can reset them. That costs less than moving a fence that ended up a few feet onto a neighbor's lot. Our guide on [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) goes through the steps.

Look for easements on the plat too. Many Smyrna lots carry a utility or drainage easement along the back or side, and the HOA or the town may limit what can sit inside it. A fence that crosses a swale should leave room at the bottom so water keeps moving. Before any hole is dug, Tennessee 811 has to be called so buried lines get marked. The call costs nothing, and Tennessee law requires it before digging.

sections.heading: Setting fence posts in Smyrna ground
paragraphs: Posts decide how long a fence stays straight. In Smyrna the auger often goes through dense clay and then hits limestone somewhere below. Clay holds water against the post, so the post needs to be rated for ground contact and set so water runs away from it instead of pooling around the wood. Where rock shows up shallow, the hole can be drilled into it or the post spacing can shift a little to find better ground. Any fence company you talk to should explain that choice before the crew starts, not after.

Gates take more strain than any other part of a fence. A wide gate on a clay lot can sag if its posts are not set deeper or heavier than the rest. If you need a gate wide enough for a mower or a small trailer, say so early so the posts on each side are planned for it.

sections.heading: Fencing a lot near Percy Priest Lake
paragraphs: Some Smyrna homes back toward Percy Priest Lake, and those yards tend to slope. A fence on a hill can be stepped, with each section level and a drop at every post, or racked so the rails follow the ground. Stepped sections leave triangle gaps at the bottom that a small dog can slip through. A racked fence hugs the grade but looks different from a flat run. Our guide to [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) explains both.

The back line on a lake lot is often the edge of Army Corps of Engineers land, not the water. A fence has to stay on your side of that line, and cutting trees or brush on Corps property to make room is not allowed without their approval. Many lakeside owners want a lower or more open style along the back to keep the view. Check what your HOA allows and where your pins are before settling on a layout.

sections.heading: Fence installation around a night shift
paragraphs: Many Smyrna households have someone working nights at the Nissan plant or on another rotating schedule. Fence installation is loudest on the days the post holes get dug. After that, hanging rails and pickets is steadier work, though a nail gun still makes plenty of noise. If someone in your house sleeps during the day, say so when you request an estimate. Then the loud days can be planned around that sleeper instead of coming as a surprise on the morning the crew starts.

People on nights sometimes hope a privacy fence will quiet the yard for daytime sleep. A wood fence blocks sight lines well, but it does little for noise from a busy road or a neighbor's mower. It does help with light. A tall solid fence can keep a neighbor's floodlight or passing headlights out of a ground floor bedroom window.

sections.heading: How wood fences age in Smyrna weather
paragraphs: Humid Middle Tennessee summers keep a wood fence damp for long stretches. Most wood fences in Smyrna subdivisions are pressure treated pine. It is strong and affordable, but it can twist or crack as it dries, and it turns gray within a season or two if left bare. Cedar is lighter and more stable, though it costs more. Posts usually fail first, right at the ground line. In newer Smyrna yards with irrigation, aim the sprinkler heads away from the fence so the bottom boards are not soaked every morning. A stain or sealer slows the graying and helps the boards shed water.

faqs.q: Does my Smyrna HOA decide which side of the fence faces out?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Many HOA covenants require the finished side to face the street or the neighbors, with the posts and rails on your side. If your covenants say nothing, facing the finished side out is still the usual courtesy, and it tends to look better from the road. A shadowbox style sidesteps the question, since it looks about the same from both sides. Check with the review committee before you order materials.

faqs.q: Can I fence all the way down to Percy Priest Lake?
faqs.a: Usually not. Around most of the lake, the land nearest the water is managed by the Army Corps of Engineers, and a private fence is not allowed on it without written permission from the Corps. Your fence has to stop at your property line, which may be some distance up the slope. Find your pins or check your survey first. If you are unsure where Corps land starts, ask the Corps office for the lake before anything is built.

faqs.q: What if my neighbor already has a fence on our shared line?
faqs.a: That is common in Smyrna subdivisions where one house fenced before the other. You can tie into the existing fence if your neighbor agrees and the HOA allows it, but then you share a fence you do not control. Some people build their own run just inside the line instead. Talk with your neighbor first and confirm where the line actually is. Any agreement should be in writing so nobody is confused when either house sells.

faqs.q: How do I keep my dog from getting under a new fence?
faqs.a: Watch the bottom edge. On a flat Smyrna yard, keep the pickets close to the grade. Where the yard slopes, stepped sections leave gaps that need filling with a racked design or a board along the bottom. Gates are the other weak spot, so a latch that closes on its own helps. Dogs that dig may need wire buried along the fence line. Mention your dog when you ask for an estimate so the layout can account for it.

faqs.q: We want a deck and a fence. Which should go in first?
faqs.a: On many Smyrna lots the side yards are narrow, and they are the only way to get lumber and equipment into the back. Building the deck first keeps that path open. If the fence has to go up first for a dog, plan a wide gate on one side so materials can still get through later. Our [Smyrna deck builder page](/deck-builder-smyrna-tn/) covers the deck side of the project.
